approach: The demo itself (plan, invented endpoint, Vault fix, approve without reading, small print) is guardrail material and only gets light trims. The time goes in three places around it: an HR preamble before the demo, two narrator passages explaining motives that the dialogue already shows, and a long second walkthrough of Brendan's process after the bot works. Cut the preamble and the motive narration, compress the walkthrough, and end sooner after the SJ conversation.

suggestions.title: Compress Brendan's process walkthrough

edits.text: The thing SJ said about the code, though. Marking its own homework. He's not wrong about it, is he?

Yeah, Nobody can do that, your brain just shuts off by line two hundred. So instead, you don't start with the code at all. You start with the plan it wrote before it touched a single file. That plan is two pages, and that's where the real decisions live. I read that like a hawk.
Yeah but, the tests that actually matter, the integration tests, I write THOSE directly into the plan, and review the output carefully and have it use a real partner sandbox, real tokens.

suggestions.why: The audience has just watched plan mode, the correction and the self-run tests in the demo. The patch-splitting history, the new-company analogy and the error-handling clause re-explain it. The plan-first idea and the integration-tests answer stay.
suggestions.keeps: The plan-first habit that s01c_l9 starts to show SJ and s20_l41 pays off ("used to reading a plan before an agent acts"). Kristina's homework question and Brendan's answer.

against.s01b_l38: The thing SJ said about the code, though. That it writes its own tests, so of course they pass. Marking its own homework. He's not wrong about it, is he?
against.s01b_l42: So, about what SJ said this morning, about reviewing 800 lines of code... Nobody can do that, your brain just shuts off by line two hundred, regardless of whether it was written by human or robot. So before, we'd split the code into smaller patches that are easier to review. But imagine you joined a new company and needed to learn how a service worked. You wouldn't read all the code, you would start with the documentation. So when it comes to AI code, you don't start with the code at all. You start here, this is the plan it wrote before it touched a single file. It's the documentation, the architecture, the tradeoffs, where the secrets go. That's two pages, and that's where the real decisions live. I read that like a hawk.
against.s01b_l46: Yeah but, the tests that actually matter, the integration tests, I write THOSE directly into the plan, and review the output carefully. I have it use a real partner sandbox, real tokens. And then it has access to any errors it generates, and part of the plan involves how to resolve and handle errors.

ifDeleted.summary: s01b is where Kristina first uses AI on stage: she builds the Slack-to-Jira bot in Cursor with Brendan, and that is the main home of guardrail 2. It also plants the setup that gets Brendan fired. He tracks his work in Linear and Kristina promises to copy it into Jira, which s19_l20 pays off. Cutting the scene leaves s11c's solo build and the s19 layoff reveal without their setup, and repairing that would mean rebuilding the demo somewhere else.

lost.what: Kristina buys into AI by using it on stage: Cursor plan mode, correcting the invented endpoint and hardcoded token, approving the install, closing PROJ-412
lost.elsewhere: s11c_l39 (her solo build echoes it, but it is staged as a repeat of this demo)

lost.what: Brendan tracks his tickets in Linear, not Jira, and Kristina promises to cross-post them herself (s01b_l27 to s01b_l32)
The Jira bot exists, with its token kept in Vault because Kristina told Cursor to put it there
The bot quietly resolves 3 linked issues that nobody reads (s01b_l36)
Kristina's motive is her promotion and a team that stops arguing (s01b_narrator_promotion, s01b_narrator_delivery)
lost.elsewhere: s06_narrator_security and s11c_l45 partly carry it

lost.what: Kristina calls it 'the future' out loud to Brendan (s01b_l49)

Brendan explains his review process (read the plan, read the risky five percent, write the integration tests into the plan) and it makes sense to Kristina. That is the contrast with s01c, where SJ will not look.
lost.elsewhere: s01c_l9 starts the same explanation, but SJ cuts it off

lost.what: Kristina considers going to HR over the degree comment and Brendan talks her out of it, calling SJ thorny but the best engineer he knows
lost.elsewhere: s01c_l2 (SJ admits the comment landed badly)

lost.what: Kristina learns that even Brendan can't get through to SJ, so she starts to see SJ as 'a challenge' (s01b_l53 to s01b_l55)

orphans.fix: Plant the Linear promise elsewhere, for example in Brendan's s01 standup update, or rewrite s19_l20 to explain the promise from scratch.

orphans.problem: 'Build a tool that cross posts Linear tickets into Jira... meaning to do this for Brendan since Friday' refers to a request the audience never heard.
'the Vault setup from the Jira bot... the sentence she had to type at it six weeks ago.' Without s01b, neither the bot nor that sentence exists on stage.
orphans.fix: Trim to: 'It asks whether the new signing secret should live in Vault. She types yes.'
